# Alla Gricia

## Ingredients

- 150 g guanciale, cut into finger-length strips
- 400 g rigatoni
- 70 g pecorino romano, finely grated
- an aggressive amount of coarsely ground black pepper
- a splash of the pasta cooking water
- salt for the boiling water

## Steps

1. Put the guanciale strips into a cold dry frying pan and bring the heat up slowly so the fat renders out gently rather than seizing.
2. Cook the strips until the edges are golden but the middle stays a little soft, then take the pan off the heat and leave all the rendered fat in it.
3. Boil the rigatoni in well-salted water until it is one minute short of al dente, then catch a mugful of the cooking water before you drain it.
4. Toast the black pepper in a small dry pan for thirty seconds, just until it smells sharp, then tip it into the rendered fat.
5. Lift the drained pasta into the frying pan with a splash of the cooking water and toss hard over low heat until the starch thickens the fat into a glossy coating.
6. Take the pan off the heat, count to ten, then stir in the pecorino romano in three additions so it melts into a sauce instead of clumping.

## Notes

There is no tomato in this dish and there is no egg in it either. People often assume every Roman pasta must contain one or the other, but here the sauce is only rendered fat, cheese and pepper, worked with a little pasta water into a smooth cream. I keep the pepper coarse rather than fine because the grains stay visible and give small bursts of heat, and I use more of it than feels sensible the first time. The rigatoni needs its ridges to hold the sauce, so smooth tubes are a poor substitute. Pecorino romano is sharper and saltier than parmesan, and that saltiness is exactly why the pan must come off the heat before the cheese goes in; a hot pan splits the fat and the cheese tightens into strings. If the sauce looks dry, add cooking water a spoonful at a time and never oil, which only makes it slide off the pasta. I serve it in warmed bowls straight away because it stiffens quickly as it cools. Leftovers are best reheated in a covered pan with a splash of water rather than a microwave, which turns the guanciale rubbery. A glass of cold dry white wine cuts the fat nicely, and a plain green salad is the only side I bother with.
